title: The machine learning workflow III: classification, experiment tracking and hyperparameter search

items.context: Most classifiers predict a category in two steps. What is the first step?
items.why:
A classifier does not jump straight to a class label. It first scores how likely each
class is, a number between 0 and 1, and only afterward turns that number into a decision
with a threshold.
items.true: Predict a probability for each class, a number between 0 and 1
false: Predict the class directly, then estimate how probable that guess is
Fit a straight line through the training data and round its output
Compare the new sample against every training sample and vote

items.context:
Logistic regression is fitted on the plant's reactor cooling water valve channel, giving
w = 7.24 per percent open and b = -314.1. Where does its decision boundary sit?
items.why:
The boundary sits where the straight-line score w x + b equals zero, so x = -b / w.
Dividing 314.1 by 7.24 gives 43.4, so the boundary is at 43.4% open, not at the raw value
of b or at a round number like 50%.
items.true: 43.4% open, where w x + b equals zero
false: 50.0% open, the midpoint of the probability scale
41.0% open, the valve's typical position during normal operation
314.1% open, the value of b read directly

items.context:
A logistic regression trained on one plant channel catches 0% of fault 14, while a
decision tree using two cuts on that same channel catches most of it. Why does the
straight cut fail here?
items.why:
Fault 14 leaves the valve's average unchanged but widens its swings, so roughly half the
fault samples sit above the normal band and half below it. A single straight cut can only
exclude one side, so whichever half it flags as normal lets the other half through, while a
tree's two cuts can bracket the normal band from both sides at once.
items.true: Its samples fall on both sides of the normal band, and one straight cut can only split off one side
false: Fault 14 never appears in the training runs, so no model could learn to catch it
The valve channel carries no information about fault 14, so only a tree can use it
A decision tree always beats logistic regression, on every channel and every fault

items.context:
Logistic regression is trained by minimizing the log loss, also called cross-entropy.
When is that loss small?
items.why:
Log loss penalizes a confident wrong guess heavily and rewards a confident correct one, so
it comes out small only when the model assigns high probability to whichever class a
sample truly belongs to.
items.true: When the model gives the true class a high probability
false: When the model's predicted probability is always exactly 0.5
When the model predicts the same class for every sample
When the weighted sum w x + b is exactly zero for every sample

items.context: A decision tree box holds 4 normal samples and 1 faulty sample. What is its Gini impurity?
items.why:
Gini impurity is 1 minus the sum of each class's squared share. With 4 of 5 samples normal
(0.8) and 1 of 5 faulty (0.2), impurity is 1 minus (0.8 squared plus 0.2 squared), which is
1 minus 0.68, or 0.32. It is 0 only when a box holds one class alone.

items.context:
A neural network's last layer produces one score per class. What does the softmax that
follows guarantee about the numbers it outputs?
items.why:
Softmax exponentiates each class score and divides by the sum of all the exponentials,
which forces every output to be positive while the whole set sums to 1, so the outputs
behave like a probability distribution over the classes.
items.true: They are positive and add up to 1
false: They are rounded to the nearest class label
Only the single largest score survives; the rest become zero
They are centered at zero, some positive and some negative

items.context:
A Gaussian process classifier turns a smooth random function into a probability through a
link function. Why is it not run on the plant's full 172,500-sample training set?
items.why:
A Gaussian process needs a kernel matrix with one row and one column per training sample,
and the memory that takes grows with the square of the sample count, which is why
172,500 plant samples would need 238 GB just to hold the matrix.
items.true: Its kernel matrix for that many samples would need 238 GB
false: It would overfit, since it has one parameter per training sample
Its link function only works with a single input channel
It needs the labels of the test runs during training

items.context:
A baseline detector always predicts "normal" and scores 85.4% accuracy on the plant's
test data. What is its recall?
items.why:
Recall counts what fraction of the real faults a model caught. A detector that never
predicts fault has zero true positives, so its recall is zero no matter how respectable
its accuracy looks.
items.true: Zero, since it never predicts a fault at all
false: 85.4%, the same as its accuracy
14.6%, the fraction of samples that are actually faulty
Undefined, since it never raises a false alarm

items.context:
Of the network's 8,313 alarms, 8,300 were real faults, and it caught 8,300 of the 8,640
real faults in the test data. What are its precision and recall?
items.why:
Precision divides the correct alarms by all the alarms raised, 8,300 over 8,313, which is
0.998. Recall divides the faults caught by all the faults that exist, 8,300 over 8,640,
which is 0.961. The two denominators differ, so there is no reason for the two fractions
to come out equal.
items.true: Precision 0.998, recall 0.961, from 8,300 correct alarms and 8,300 of 8,640 faults caught
false: Precision 0.961, recall 0.998, from swapping which count divides which total
Precision 0.998, recall 0.998, since both counts share the same numerator of 8,300
Precision 0.961, recall 0.961, since precision and recall must always agree

items.context:
The plant's classifier calls a sample a fault, but the sample was in fact normal. Which box
of the confusion matrix does that sample land in?
items.why:
"Positive" is what the model said, a fault, and "false" says it was wrong. So a normal
sample the model called a fault is a false positive, a false alarm. A false negative is
the other mistake: a fault the model called normal.
false: False negative (FN): a missed fault
True positive (TP): a fault caught
True negative (TN): a normal sample left alone

items.context:
A scikit-learn classifier offers both a predict method and a predict_proba method for the
same sample. What is the difference?
items.why:
predict is the class decision itself, reached by comparing the probability to 0.5 by
default. predict_proba hands back the probability underneath that decision, which is what
lets you choose a different threshold instead of accepting the default.
items.true: predict returns a class using a 0.5 threshold; predict_proba returns each class's probability
false: predict returns a probability; predict_proba returns a class using a 0.5 threshold
predict only works with two classes; predict_proba works with any number of classes
predict needs labeled training data; predict_proba needs no labels at all

items.context:
The plant's neural network classifier has its threshold lowered from 0.50 to 0.01. What
happens to its recall and its precision?
items.why:
A lower threshold flags more samples as faulty, so it catches more of the real faults,
raising recall, while also raising more false alarms, lowering precision. There is no
threshold that improves both at once.
items.true: Recall rises toward 0.977 and precision falls toward 0.697
false: Recall falls toward 0.697 and precision rises toward 0.977
Both rise, since a lower threshold flags more faults without adding false alarms
Neither changes; the threshold only relabels samples, not the rates

items.context:
Different thresholds trade recall against precision by different amounts. How should a
team pick which threshold to use?
items.why:
No single threshold is best in general, since lowering it always trades fewer missed
faults for more false alarms. The right choice depends on what each kind of mistake
actually costs in the plant, not on a fixed rule or a single summary score.
items.true: From the relative cost of a missed fault against the cost of a false alarm
false: Always at 0.5, since that is what scikit-learn uses by default
At whichever threshold gives the highest accuracy
At whichever threshold makes precision and recall exactly equal

items.context:
A network trained on nine plant faults is then tested on eight faults it never saw during
training. What happens to its recall across those eight?
items.why:
Some unseen faults happen to resemble a trained fault closely enough that the network
still catches most of them, while others resemble nothing it has seen and are almost
entirely missed. Nothing in its training scores predicts in advance which end a new fault
will land on.
items.true: It ranges from 0.924 on one fault down to 0.001 on another
false: It stays close to its trained recall of 0.961 on every one of them
It is exactly zero on all eight, since none of them were in training
It settles near 0.5 on all eight, since the network is only guessing

items.context:
A team reports their network's 96.1% recall on the nine faults it was trained on as proof
it will catch whatever fault the plant develops next. What is missing from that claim?
items.why:
A recall measured on the faults a network was trained on says nothing about a fault it has
never seen, since a supervised classifier can only recognize the classes it was trained on.
The only way to find out how it handles a genuinely new fault is to hold one out on purpose
and test against it.
items.true: Recognition that it only knows the faults it was trained on, and a test against a fault it never saw
false: A comparison against the accuracy of a baseline that always predicts normal
A second network trained on the same nine faults with a different random seed
More training samples drawn from the same nine faults it already knows

items.context:
Bergstra and Bengio (2012) argue that random search beats a grid search at the same trial
budget. What is their reasoning?
items.why:
A grid spends equal effort on every hyperparameter, including ones that barely affect the
score, so most of its trials repeat values of something that does not matter much. Random
search, at the same budget, samples many distinct values along every axis, so it explores
whichever one matters more thoroughly without needing to know which one that is in advance.
items.true: Usually only a few hyperparameters matter, and random search tries more distinct values of those
false: Random search always evaluates fewer total configurations, leaving a larger budget per trial
A grid cannot represent an integer-valued hyperparameter such as a tree's maximum depth
Random search is guaranteed to eventually find the single best configuration

items.context:
Optuna's default sampler, TPE, uses past trials to guide future ones. In the search on the
concrete strength dataset, how did its first guided trial compare with random search?
items.why:
TPE builds a model of which hyperparameter values look promising from the trials run so
far, so once it has a handful of trials to learn from, it can aim its very next guess
there instead of guessing blindly. Random search has no such model, so it keeps guessing
uniformly and takes far longer to reach a similarly good score.
items.true: TPE's first guided trial, trial 11, already scored 8.90 MPa; random search took 38 trials to reach 9.00 MPa
false: TPE's first guided trial matched random search exactly, both reaching 8.90 MPa at trial 11
TPE needed 38 trials to reach 8.90 MPa, the same count random search needed for 9.00 MPa
Random search reached 8.90 MPa before TPE did, since TPE's early trials are random too

items.context:
An Optuna study finishes, and its winning configuration is refit and registered in
MLflow's model registry. What does that registry give a teammate that the winning trial's
own child run does not?
items.why:
A child run is tied to the one trial that produced it, one among possibly dozens, so
finding the winner later means remembering which run it was. The registry instead gives
the winning model its own name and version, loadable by anyone later with no memory of the
search required.
items.true: A name and version they can load later, without needing to remember which trial won
false: A live connection that keeps retraining the model as new data arrives
A guarantee that this model will outperform every future search
A bundled copy of every losing trial's hyperparameters alongside the winner's

items.context:
A team's Optuna search on the concrete strength dataset finds a best validation RMSE of
8.90 MPa over many trials, and reports that number as their model's expected performance
on new data. What is wrong?
items.why:
The validation score comes from the same rows the search used to pick a winner, so it is
the number the search was tuned against, not an honest estimate of new data. Scoring the
registered winner once on mixes that never took part in the search is what gives the
number to report.
items.true: The search chose its winner by that number; the registered winner's test score, 7.41 MPa, is the one to report
false: Nothing is wrong; grouped cross-validation already accounts for the search, so 8.90 MPa is unbiased
The number should have come from a grid search instead of from TPE
Forty trials is too few for TPE to have found a trustworthy best score
